paras: The attempted lynching of John Newton took place in May 1888 at the jail in Washington, Beaufort County, North Carolina, where a mob gathered to lynch Newton, a white man accused of complicity in the murder of the lumberman Joshua A. Cox. The jail was strongly guarded and the mob abandoned its plan, and Newton was later tried and convicted as an accessory after the fact. The attempt followed the lynching of Cox's accused killer, Thomas Frazier, a few days earlier.

According to the Washington Gazette, Frazier shot Cox at Blount's Creek, sixteen miles from Washington, on a Saturday in early May after Cox refused to sell him liquor, using a gun taken from one of his two companions, "Newton and Adams." Before dawn masked men overpowered the guard over Frazier, took him out and shot him dead, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict of death at the hands of parties unknown.

Newton and W. B. Adams, described as accessories to the murder, fled armed into the swamps of Blount's Creek after a deputy and posse went after them. On affidavit both men were outlawed, "any citizen empowered to take them dead or alive," while "the whole community" was reported in arms against them.

Newton was captured by mid-May and lodged in the Washington jail, while Adams remained in hiding. A Raleigh correspondent wrote that it had been "believed at first" that both men would be lynched as soon as they were taken. Within a few nights of the capture a mob gathered at the jail, but, in the Reflector's words, "the jail was guarded" and "the design of the mob defeated." The Raleigh account added that the lynchers' plans were abandoned "at the last moment."

In early June a grand jury found a true bill for murder against John M. Newton, and a Raleigh special then reported that several attempts to lynch him had failed. In December the Richmond Dispatch reported that Newton had been tried in Beaufort County, convicted of being accessory after the fact and given seven years in the penitentiary. He appealed to the state Supreme Court, but could not give the $15,000 bail set for him. No report of arrests of the would-be lynchers, or of Adams's capture, appears in the coverage.

The attempt reached print only as short items inside larger news columns. The Richmond Dispatch carried it in a Raleigh telegram headed "DEATH-WARRANT.," and the Edenton Fisherman & Farmer reprinted the Reflector's account under "CAPTURED." Neither commented on the would-be lynchers, and the Reflector turned at once to the posse still hunting Adams.

The Raleigh State Chronicle had called the earlier Frazier lynching "Disgraceful," but no comparable comment on the attempt against Newton appears. The Atlanta Constitution mentioned the failed attempts in one sentence of a June item headed "Joshua Cox's Murderers." Only the last Dispatch note identified Newton's race, calling him "white."

The May reports describe a single mob at the jail, while the June Raleigh special speaks of "several attempts." That June report also named the second fugitive "Thomas Adams," where the local and Raleigh papers gave W. B. Adams.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Newton
bases: A mob gathered at the Washington jail to lynch the prisoner Newton but was turned back by guards (A6, A7), an attempted lynching.

Newton was not killed; a 'mob' gathered to lynch him in jail over his alleged part in the Cox murder but abandoned its plan because the jail was guarded (A6, A7), and he was later tried and convicted (A9, A10). It was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
A Raleigh telegram (A6) and the local Reflector (A7) independently report the failed mob attempt at the jail, and a later Raleigh special (A8) mentions attempts to lynch him.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondent (May 19)
accounts.gist: An attempt was made a few nights earlier to lynch Newton, but the jail was so strongly guarded that the lynchers abandoned their plans at the last moment.

accounts.label: Local press (the Reflector)
accounts.gist: Newton was captured and lodged in Washington jail; a mob gathered to lynch him but the guard defeated its design.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondent (June 5)
accounts.gist: Several attempts to lynch Newton had failed; he had been indicted for murder.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch placed the attempt in a Raleigh news roundup under 'DEATH-WARRANT.', noting it had been 'believed at first' that Newton and Adams would be lynched on capture.
The Reflector, reprinted under 'CAPTURED.', reported the mob's 'design' defeated without comment and looked forward to Adams's capture.
The Raleigh State Chronicle closed its report of the related Frazier lynching with the word 'Disgraceful.'
The Atlanta Constitution's 'Joshua Cox's Murderers.' item mentioned the failed attempts in one sentence.

conflicts.note: The later June 5 report may include attempts after the first reports, or may generalize; the earlier, local account (A7) describes a single mob.
The local Gazette and Raleigh reports agree on W. B. Adams; the Atlanta version probably confuses him with Thomas Frazier.
